chapters.title: The Text Workshop
chapters.scope: Open with a recap strip, not a re-teach: strings are immutable sequences you can index and slice (ch7), + and * and len (ch3), quotes and \n escapes (ch1), split() and join() basics (ch7), f-string holes (ch2), :.2f and , (ch3). Then, in order. (1) Gap fill from B8: raw strings r'...' (backslashes kept), triple-quoted multi-line strings. (2) Methods vs functions: s.upper() is called on the string, len(s) takes it as an argument; methods return a NEW string, so s.upper() on its own leaves s unchanged (no error, the classic silent bug: forgot to reassign after .strip()). (3) Case: upper, lower, title, capitalize, casefold (for caseless comparison; 'Z' < 'a' recap from ch4). (4) Whitespace: strip, lstrip, rstrip. (5) split with no argument (splits on runs of whitespace and drops empty pieces: ' a  b '.split() gives ['a', 'b']) vs split(',') (keeps empty fields: 'a,,b' gives ['a', '', 'b']); join needs strings: ','.join([1, 2]) gives TypeError: sequence item 0: expected str instance, int found. (6) replace. (7) Searching: find returns -1 on a miss, index raises ValueError: substring not found; count, startswith, endswith. (8) Tests: isdigit, isalpha, isspace, isupper (use isdigit to check typed input before int()). (9) Chaining methods left to right; iterating characters; building a string from pieces with a list and ''.join instead of repeated +=. (10) ord and chr; Unicode characters and most emoji have len 1. Wrong-method errors: 'abc'.append('d') gives AttributeError: 'str' object has no attribute 'append'; 'abc'.lenght() gives AttributeError: 'str' object has no attribute 'lenght'. (11) Formatting (B10): f-strings recap, any expression in the braces; the format-spec mini-language after the colon: width, alignment < > ^, fill character, precision .2f, thousands ',', percent '%', zero padding 05d / 03d; f'{3.14159:.2f}', f'{42:>5}', f'{7:03d}'; the self-documenting {x=} form (met in ch9 as a debugging tool); str() vs repr() and the !r / !s / !a conversions; escaping literal braces with {{ }}; reusing the same quote inside an f-string is allowed from 3.12; str.format() and % formatting as read-only awareness. Formatting errors: f'{"abc":d}' gives ValueError: Unknown format code 'd' for object of type 'str'; f'{name!z}' gives SyntaxError: f-string: invalid conversion character 'z': expected 's', 'r', or 'a'; forgetting the f prints the braces literally (no error); '{name}'.format(nam='x') gives KeyError: 'name'. Close with a project: a receipt or scoreboard whose columns line up, cleaned from messy typed input.

chapters.title: Boxes Inside Boxes
chapters.scope: Recap pointers only: lists, tuples, unpacking and enumerate (ch7), dicts, sets and counting (ch8), with open, modes and the home-made comma format (ch10), the recipe book's dict of dicts (ch10). Then, in order. (1) Gap fill from B21: zip pairs two lists and stops at the shortest; zip(..., strict=True) raises when the lengths differ (capture the real ValueError); star unpacking first, *rest = ...; for name, score in zip(names, scores); for k, v in d.items(); tuples as dict keys (grid coordinates). (2) The four shapes: list of dicts (records), dict of lists (groups), dict of dicts (lookup by id), list of lists (grid, recap). (3) Index paths read left to right: data[0]['name'], step-by-step what each bracket hands back; deep indexes are easy to get wrong silently. (4) Walking nested data with nested loops; the grouping pattern (start an empty list for a new key, then append) next to the counting pattern from ch8; setdefault as awareness. (5) Classic mistakes: data[0]['name'] on a dict of lists gives a KeyError: 0 (or a TypeError on the wrong layer); for k, v in d: instead of d.items() gives ValueError: too many values to unpack (expected 2) for string keys longer than 2 characters, while 2-character keys silently unpack into their letters. (6) Gap fill from B19: copies of nested data are shallow: .copy() of a list of lists shares the inner lists; copy.deepcopy makes independent copies; grid = [[0]*3]*3; grid[0][0] = 1 changes every row (no error), and the safe way to build a grid with a loop. (7) Choosing a structure by asking: does order matter? must items be unique? do I look things up by a key? is the shape fixed? list vs tuple vs dict vs set, with five small scenarios. (8) Data that looks like JSON, then gap fill from B26 on the main path: json.dump / json.load with indent=2 (a round trip keeps ints as ints; int dict keys come back as strings: json.dumps({1: 'a'}) gives {"1": "a"}); json.loads("{'a': 1}") gives json.decoder.JSONDecodeError: Expecting property name enclosed in double quotes: line 1 column 2 (char 1); csv.reader and csv.DictReader with newline='' and encoding='utf-8' (fixes ch10's 'mac, cheese' problem); DictReader rows are dicts, so a CSV file becomes a list of dicts, and every value is a string until you convert it; pathlib.Path basics: joining with /, exists(), read_text / write_text. (9) Project: a small gradebook or inventory loaded from CSV, grouped, reported, saved as JSON. End with 'when a dict of fields wants to become a class' as a teaser for ch15.

chapters.title: Borrowing Toolboxes
chapters.scope: (1) Modules as toolboxes on a shelf: import math; math.sqrt; from math import sqrt; import statistics as st; why from x import * is avoided (names appear from nowhere, can shadow yours). (2) A tour of everyday modules: math, random (randint, choice, shuffle, seed; with random.seed(1), three randint(1, 6) calls printed 2 5 1 on both versions), datetime basics (date, today), statistics (mean, median), sys (sys.version, sys.argv first look), os (getcwd). (3) dir() and help() on a module (help() was met in ch6). (4) Your own module: helpers.py next to main.py, import helpers, call helpers.f; if __name__ == '__main__': and why: the classic bug where importing a module runs its demo code. (5) The module search path at a basic level: the script's folder first, then the standard library, then installed packages; so a file named random.py beside your script breaks import random: AttributeError: module 'random' has no attribute 'randint' (consider renaming '.../random.py' since it has the same name as the standard library module named 'random' and prevents importing that standard library module) (link back to ch2's file-naming advice). (6) Import errors: import requestz gives ModuleNotFoundError: No module named 'requestz'; from math import sqroot gives ImportError: cannot import name 'sqroot' from 'math' (unknown location). Did you mean: 'sqrt'?; unseeded random changes output every run. 3.15's lazy import as one-line awareness. (7) B28: the standard library vs third-party packages; PyPI; python -m pip install NAME and why python -m pip rather than bare pip (it installs into the Python you will run); pip list, pip uninstall. (8) Virtual environments as a separate pantry per project: python -m venv .venv, activating and deactivating on Windows (.venv\Scripts\activate), macOS and Linux (source .venv/bin/activate), how the prompt changes, requirements.txt and pip install -r; why not install globally; recent Linux and macOS system Pythons refuse global pip installs with an externally-managed-environment message. (9) uv as a fast all-in-one alternative (uv venv, uv add, uv run) and pyproject.toml as awareness. (10) Classic mistakes: installing into one Python and running another, or forgetting to activate the venv, both give ModuleNotFoundError: No module named '...'; the editor using a different interpreter than the terminal.

chapters.title: Smoke Alarms and Blueprints
chapters.scope: Recap: ch9 wrote tiny assert tests and listed the debugging kit; build on them. (1) Why test: a test is a smoke alarm, cheap to install and loud before the fire spreads; a test that can never fail is useless. (2) Test functions named test_..., plain assert, running python -m pytest, reading pytest's dots/F and the failure report (the diff of expected vs actual). (3) Arrange-act-assert. (4) Edge cases: empty, zero, negative, very large; the function that passes the happy-path test but fails the empty-list test. (5) pytest.raises to test that bad input raises the right exception. (6) Separating logic from input/output so functions are testable (pull the calculation out of the input() loop). (7) Red-green-refactor. (8) Floats: == fails for 0.1 + 0.2 (ch3), use pytest.approx or math.isclose. (9) assert (x, 'msg') is always true and prints SyntaxWarning: assertion is always true, perhaps remove parentheses?; doctest as awareness. (10) Gap fill from B17: stepping through a failing test with a debugger: breakpoint() and the (Pdb) prompt with n, s, p, c, q; the editor debugger's breakpoints, step over / into / out, watch and call-stack panels (screenshots-free description with a lab); leaving breakpoint() in a script makes it pause. (11) B30: reading the docs: docs.python.org layout (tutorial, library reference, glossary); reading a signature such as sorted(iterable, /, *, key=None, reverse=False) at the reading level (what the / and * mean is taught in ch17; misreading them leads to a TypeError about positional-only arguments passed as keywords); help(), dir(), type() at the prompt. (12) PEP 8 style beyond names: line length, spacing, blank lines; PEPs in general. (13) Decomposing a problem: pseudocode, top-down decomposition into function stubs, incremental development (run after every few lines; big-bang coding produces many errors at once), the LEGO-bags picture; asking good questions (refer to ch9's help template) and using AI assistants critically (check claims, run the code, read the error yourself). (14) Project: build a small tool (e.g. a word-statistics or password-rules checker) from pseudocode to stubs to tests to code, red-green each step.

chapters.title: Cookie Cutters
chapters.scope: (1) Gap fill from B19 first: everything is an object; id() and is ('same object?') vs == ('equal?'), revisiting ch2's notebook question; 'changing' an int or str makes a new object while list methods change the same object; passing a list to a function lets the function mutate the caller's list, but reassigning the parameter inside the function does not affect the caller; removing items from a list while looping over it skips items (no error), so loop over a copy or build a new list; mutating a dict while looping gives RuntimeError: dictionary changed size during iteration. (2) Methods are functions attached to objects (s.upper(), xs.append() seen before). (3) class: a cookie cutter; instances: the cookies. (4) __init__ and self ('this particular cookie'); instance attributes set as self.name = name; methods that read and change attributes; calling p.greet() is really Pet.greet(p). (5) __str__ and __repr__ for printing; printing an object without them shows <__main__.A object at 0x...> and the address changes every run. (6) Objects as bundles of data and behaviour; when a dict record from ch12 should become a class. (7) Classic errors: forgetting self in a method gives TypeError: A.hi() takes 0 positional arguments but 1 was given; a typo __init_ gives TypeError: A() takes no arguments; reading an attribute that was never set gives AttributeError: 'A' object has no attribute 'name'; forgetting self. inside a method (name = name) stores nothing on the object. (8) Project: rebuild the ch10 recipe or the ch12 gradebook record as a class with two or three methods, then a short beginner-track graduation recap pointing to the intermediate part.
chapters.not_yet: Class attributes, @property, @classmethod/@staticmethod, name mangling (ch19); inheritance and composition (ch19); dunder methods beyond __init__/__str__/__repr__ (ch20); dataclasses (ch20); type hints (ch21).
chapters.visuals: (1) Cookie-cutter picture: one cutter (class), several cookies (instances) each with its own icing (attributes). (2) Memory tracer: two instances as object boxes with their own attributes and a shared class box; the tracer has no 'instance' kind, so draw attributes as dict-style pairs labelled with the class name, or request an 'object' kind from the engine. (3) Memory tracer for the B19 gap: a function frame whose parameter points at the caller's list, mutation vs reassignment. (4) Method-call machine: p.greet() unfolds to Pet.greet(p), the self arrow pointing at the cookie.

chapters.title: Lazy Conveyor Belts
chapters.scope: (1) Gap fill from B12: the conditional expression a if c else b, needed for comprehension transforms. (2) I1 comprehensions as a factory line in one sentence: [expression for x in source if condition]; filtering with if; transforming with x if c else y placed BEFORE the for (putting else after the for part is a SyntaxError); nested comprehensions read in the same order as the nested loops they replace; dict and set comprehensions; a generator expression preview; when a plain loop is clearer, and the two-part limit (no more than two for/if parts); side-effect comprehensions like [print(x) for x in xs] build a useless list; comprehension variables do not leak; 3.15 allows unpacking in comprehensions [*L for L in lists], which in 3.13 gives SyntaxError: iterable unpacking cannot be used in comprehension. (3) I2 the iteration protocol: iterable vs iterator; iter() and next(); StopIteration at the end; what for does underneath (ch5's notebook said 'for asks for the next item'); iterators are single-use; lazy objects: range, map, zip, dict views; built-in iteration tools: enumerate, zip(strict=True) recaps, reversed, sorted with key and reverse (key=len, key=str.lower; lambdas come in ch17), map, filter, any, all, sum, min/max with key and default. Errors: next(it) past the end gives StopIteration; looping over an object with no __iter__ gives TypeError: 'Bag' object is not iterable (use a ch15-style class; making it iterable is ch20); reusing a map or zip object yields nothing the second time (no error); sum(['a', 'b']) gives TypeError: unsupported operand type(s) for +: 'int' and 'str'. (4) I3 generators: yield; generator functions vs return; calling a generator function runs nothing and only returns a generator object; lazy evaluation and the memory benefit; generator expressions; exhaustion: list(g) twice gives [0, 1, 4] then [] (no error); yield from; infinite generators; pipelines of generators. (5) itertools: count, cycle, islice, chain, groupby (needs sorted input, or it splits groups silently), product, permutations, combinations, accumulate, batched (3.12+), pairwise.
chapters.not_yet: lambda and key functions in depth (ch17), __iter__/__next__ on your own classes (ch20), async generators (ch27), measuring speed and memory (ch24), Counter/defaultdict (ch23).
chapters.visuals: (1) Factory-line picture: source belt (for), quality-control gate (if), stamping machine (expression), with each part of a real comprehension labelled by word and position, not colour alone. (2) Candy-dispenser picture: the packet is the iterable, the loaded dispenser is the iterator, one candy per next() click until StopIteration (a machine whose last example jams with the real StopIteration). (3) Storyteller walker: a generator and its consumer printing interleaved lines, stepping shows where the generator pauses at yield and resumes; the final screen equals the real output. (4) Generator pipeline map: read -> filter -> transform -> take, showing that nothing moves until the last stage pulls.

Avoid sys.getsizeof numbers as answer keys (they vary by version/build). Infinite generators must be cut with islice so the run ends inside the 10 s limit.

chapters.title: Machines as Parcels
chapters.scope: (1) I4 functions are values (ch6's notebook: def is an assignment): assign a function to another name, pass it as an argument, return it, store functions in a dict as a dispatch table; callbacks. (2) lambda: a single-expression anonymous function; assigning a lambda to a name is a style smell (use def). (3) Key functions: sorted(key=...), max(key=...), min(key=...) with lambdas and with operator.itemgetter / attrgetter. (4) map and filter vs comprehensions (ch16); functools.reduce; functools.partial. (5) Pure functions and immutability as the functional mindset (ch6 introduced pure functions). Errors: sorted(xs, key=len()) gives TypeError: len() takes exactly one argument (0 given) because the function was called instead of passed; x = 5; x() gives TypeError: 'int' object is not callable. (6) I5 advanced parameters: *args collects extra positional arguments into a tuple; **kwargs collects extra keyword arguments into a dict; keyword-only parameters after *; positional-only parameters before /; unpacking at the call site f(*xs), f(**d); now read sorted(iterable, /, *, key=None, reverse=False) fully (ch14 only read it). (7) The mutable default trap: def f(x, acc=[]) called twice returns [1] then [1, 2] (no error) because defaults are evaluated once, when def runs; the None sentinel default fix; 3.15's sentinel builtin as awareness. Errors: f(1, 2) for def f(a, *, b) gives TypeError: f() takes 1 positional argument but 2 were given; f(a=1) for def f(a, /) gives TypeError: f() got some positional-only arguments passed as keyword arguments: 'a'.
chapters.not_yet: Closures, nonlocal and late binding (ch18), decorators (ch18), Callable type hints (ch21), functools.cache (ch18).
chapters.visuals: (1) Recipe-card picture: a function handed to another cook to use with their own ingredients. (4) Shared tip-jar memory tracer for the mutable default: the function object holds one default list, two calls drop coins into the same jar; then the None-sentinel version with a fresh jar each call. Plus a signature slot board showing the positional-only | normal | keyword-only zones around / and *.

chapters.title: Backpacks and Gift Wrap
chapters.scope: (1) I6 nested functions and the enclosing scope; LEGB completed (ch6 gave the basic version); closures capture variables, not values: the backpack the inner function carries, which also sees later changes; nonlocal to rebind an enclosing variable; assigning without nonlocal gives UnboundLocalError: cannot access local variable ... where it is not associated with a value (ch6 showed the global version); global vs nonlocal; factories (counter, multiplier); late binding in loops: [lambda: i for i in range(3)] called gives [2, 2, 2] (no error); fixing it by binding early with a default argument (ties to ch17: defaults are evaluated at def time); currying as awareness. (2) I7 decorators: a function that takes a function and returns a wrapper; @ syntax as shorthand for f = deco(f); decoration time vs call time (what prints when); preserving metadata with functools.wraps (without it __name__ shows 'wrapper'); decorators with arguments (three layers); stacking order (bottom decorator applies first) and how the wrong order changes behaviour silently; timing and logging decorators; built-in decorators: @functools.cache and @lru_cache (with cache_info()), preview of @property, @classmethod, @staticmethod (taught in ch19); class decorators as awareness. Errors: forgetting return wrapper gives TypeError: 'NoneType' object is not callable when the decorated function is called.
chapters.not_yet: @property/@classmethod/@staticmethod in depth (ch19), @dataclass (ch20), recursion with @cache (ch24), measuring time properly with timeit (ch24), logging module (ch26).
chapters.visuals: (1) Backpack picture: the inner function leaves home with a backpack of enclosing variables. (2) Memory tracer with frames: the counter factory's frame stays alive because the returned function still refers to it; nonlocal rebinding visible as a moved arrow. (3) Gift-wrap picture: the present (function) is unchanged, callers open the wrapper first; stacked wrappers drawn as layers matching the @ lines. (4) Print-order walker: a decorated program stepping through decoration time (at import) then call time, final screen equal to the real output; a late-binding tracer showing three lambdas pointing at one i.

chapters.title: Family Trees and Toolbelts
chapters.scope: (1) I9 instance attributes vs class attributes: the shared office whiteboard vs each person's notebook; assigning through an instance creates an instance attribute that hides the class one; the shared mutable class attribute trap (a list as a class attribute is shared by all instances, no error). (2) @property getters and setters, validation in setters; assigning to a read-only property gives AttributeError: property 'c' of 'T' object has no setter. (3) Encapsulation conventions: _internal and __mangled names. (4) @classmethod alternative constructors (from_string), @staticmethod helpers; choosing between them. (5) __repr__ vs __str__ deepened (ch15); objects holding other objects; methods calling methods; __slots__ as awareness: AttributeError: 'P' object has no attribute 'y' and no __dict__ for setting new attributes. (6) I10 subclassing and overriding; super().__init__(); forgetting it gives AttributeError: 'B' object has no attribute 'a'; method resolution order and how Python climbs the tree; isinstance and issubclass; duck typing and polymorphism through shared method names; abstract base classes with abc.ABC and @abstractmethod: instantiating one gives TypeError: Can't instantiate abstract class S without an implementation for abstract method 'area'; composition vs inheritance ('has-a' vs 'is-a') and why deep trees that should be composition hurt; mixins as awareness; collections.abc for custom containers (a pointer to ch20).
chapters.not_yet: Dunder methods for operators, len, iteration, hashing (ch20), dataclasses (ch20), Protocol and type hints (ch21), custom exception hierarchies (ch22).

(2) Family-tree map: attribute lookup climbing the MRO, each path checked against a real program that prints which method ran. (3) Property gatekeeper machine: setting a value goes through the setter; an invalid value jams with the real ValueError; assigning a read-only property jams with the real AttributeError. (4) Toolbelt picture for composition (an object holding parts) beside the family tree for inheritance; a choice exercise per scenario.

chapters.title: Sockets and Stamped Forms
chapters.scope: (1) I11 the data model: special ('dunder') methods are what syntax calls: len(obj) calls obj.__len__(), obj[i] calls __getitem__, x in obj calls __contains__, for calls __iter__ (finally make ch16's Bag iterable); __bool__ and truthiness; __eq__ and __hash__: defining __eq__ removes hashability, so the object can no longer go in a set or be a dict key; ordering with __lt__ and functools.total_ordering; arithmetic with __add__ and __radd__, returning NotImplemented (returning False instead silently breaks reflected operations); __call__; __repr__ conventions (looks like the constructor call); protocols as informal interfaces. (2) I12 @dataclass: fields with defaults, the auto-generated __init__, __repr__ and ==; field(default_factory=list); xs: list = [] gives ValueError: mutable default <class 'list'> for field xs is not allowed: use default_factory; frozen=True and changing a field gives dataclasses.FrozenInstanceError: cannot assign to field 'x'; order=True; slots=True; a dataclass with eq=True is not hashable: {P(1)} gives TypeError: cannot use 'P' as a set element (unhashable type: 'P') (3.13: TypeError: unhashable type: 'P'). (3) typing.NamedTuple and collections.namedtuple. (4) enum.Enum, auto, IntEnum, Flag, iterating an enum; C(5) for an invalid value gives ValueError: 5 is not a valid C. (5) frozendict, a new builtin in 3.15 (in 3.13: NameError: name 'frozendict' is not defined. Did you mean: 'frozenset'?). (6) Choosing between dict, tuple, NamedTuple, dataclass and a full class; sum types as awareness.
chapters.not_yet: Type hints beyond the dataclass field annotations (ch21; say here that the annotations are labels Python does not enforce), match/case class patterns (ch21), descriptors and metaclasses (beyond this book).

(4) Decision map for record types (need to change it? need a name per field? need methods? need hashing?) ending in dict / NamedTuple / dataclass / frozen dataclass / class.

chapters.title: Labels and Sorting Chutes
chapters.scope: (1) I13 type hints as labels on storage boxes: the shipping company (mypy) checks them, the boxes do not care. Annotation syntax for variables, parameters and return values; built-in generics list[int], dict[str, int]; union types written with | (3.10+) and Optional; Any; Callable; TypedDict; Protocol (ties to ch20's protocols); generics and TypeVar as awareness with 3.12's def f[T] syntax. (2) Hints are not enforced at runtime: passing a str where int is hinted runs fine; running mypy (and pyright as an alternative) reports error: Argument 1 to "f" has incompatible type "str"; expected "int" (wording varies by mypy version). (3) Deferred evaluation of annotations in 3.14 (PEP 649/749): forward references needed quotes before 3.14. Pydantic for runtime validation as awareness. (4) I24 structural pattern matching as a sorting office: match/case; literal patterns; capture patterns; the wildcard _; sequence patterns; mapping patterns (matching ch12-style nested dicts); class patterns (dataclasses from ch20); OR patterns; guards with if; as bindings; when if/elif is simpler; 3.15 allows unary plus in literal patterns. Errors: case y: before other cases gives SyntaxError: name capture 'y' makes remaining patterns unreachable; expecting case RED: to compare against a variable (it captures; use a dotted name like Color.RED from ch20's enums).

chapters.title: Alarms and Key Cards
chapters.scope: Recap pointers: ch9's exception family tree, bare except, EAFP vs LBYL, keep try small, assert vs raise, except A, B without parentheses (3.14+). (1) I14 BaseException vs Exception and why except Exception still swallows bugs; custom exception classes and one root exception per package; raise ... from e prints both tracebacks joined by 'The above exception was the direct cause of the following exception'; implicit chaining when an except block itself fails; add_note(): the note prints on its own line under the message (ValueError: x, then 'while parsing row 3'); ExceptionGroup and except*, with the boxed tree of sub-exceptions in the traceback; returning None vs raising (prefer raising); finally containing return/break now warns (3.14, PEP 765); logging errors instead of printing (one-line preview; the logging module is ch26); the traceback module for formatting a caught error. (2) I15 context managers: with as guaranteed setup and teardown, the hotel key card; files (ch10), locks and temporary directories as examples; writing __enter__ and __exit__; suppressing an exception by returning True from __exit__; contextlib.contextmanager with yield; forgetting the yield gives TypeError: 'NoneType' object is not an iterator; code after yield does not run on error unless wrapped in try/finally; contextlib.suppress, closing, ExitStack, redirect_stdout; several managers in one with using the parenthesised form; using a file after its with block ends gives ValueError: I/O operation on closed file.

chapters.title: The Hardware Store
chapters.scope: Recap pointers: ch13's import styles, __name__ guard, search path, venv and pip. (1) I16 packages as a building with floors (subpackages) and rooms (modules): a folder with __init__.py; absolute vs relative imports; sys.path and how the script's folder is added; running modules with python -m package.module; a relative import in a script run directly gives ImportError: attempted relative import with no known parent package; circular imports between a.py and b.py give ImportError: cannot import name 'g' from 'b' (consider renaming '.../b.py' if it has the same name as a library you intended to import), a misleading hint in both 3.13 and 3.15, and how to break the cycle; namespace packages as awareness; the src/ layout; pyproject.toml (project metadata, dependencies, scripts); building and installing a local package in editable mode; uv and Poetry project workflows; 3.15 lazy imports (lazy import json) for startup time, which is SyntaxError: invalid syntax before 3.15; -I isolated mode removes the script folder from sys.path. (2) I17 the standard library as a hardware store: collections (Counter with most_common, defaultdict(list) grouping replacing ch12's manual pattern, deque, OrderedDict, ChainMap); functools and itertools recaps (ch16-18); pathlib in depth; datetime, timedelta, zoneinfo, naive vs aware datetimes: comparing them gives TypeError: can't compare offset-naive and offset-aware datetimes; time; json in depth (ch12 recap) and json.dumps({1, 2}) gives TypeError: Object of type set is not JSON serializable; csv; random vs secrets (never random for passwords); math, statistics, decimal (Decimal(0.1) prints 0.1000000000000000055511151231257827021181583404541015625, use Decimal('0.1'); ties to ch3's 0.1 + 0.2), fractions; heapq; bisect; shutil, os, glob; copy; pprint; textwrap; string.Template and t-strings (3.14) as awareness.

chapters.title: Dolls and Stopwatches
chapters.scope: Placed late on purpose: recursion only needs ch6 frames and ch9 tracebacks, and pairing it with performance lets memoization, merge sort and Big-O meet ch23's collections. (1) I8 recursion as Russian nesting dolls: base case and recursive case; the call stack growing frame by frame (ch6 frames); tracing recursive calls with indentation and a call tree for fib(4); prints before vs after the recursive call; recursion on numbers, strings, lists, nested structures (ch12's nested data) and trees; recursion vs iteration; the default recursion limit (1000); a missing base case gives RecursionError: maximum recursion depth exceeded after [Previous line repeated 996 more times]; forgetting to return the recursive call returns None; memoization with functools.cache (ch18); divide and conquer: binary search and merge sort. (2) I22 performance: measure first; timeit (and why one run is noise); profiling with cProfile and 3.15's profiling package (profiling.tracing, profiling.sampling 'Tachyon'); the profile module is deprecated in 3.15 (removal in 3.17); Big-O intuition as how the party queue grows (constant, linear, quadratic, log); list vs set membership (x in big_list inside a loop is quadratic, no error, just slow), dict lookup cost; string building with join vs s += piece; deque for queues; generators for memory (ch16); sys.getsizeof and tracemalloc; functools.cache revisited; when to reach for NumPy (awareness).
chapters.not_yet: Concurrency for speed (ch27), C extensions and NumPy in depth (beyond this book), advanced algorithms and data structures (beyond this book).

chapters.title: Stencils and Codebooks
chapters.scope: Recap pointer: ch11's string methods (try them before regex). (1) I18 regular expressions as a stencil slid along the text until it fits: re.search, re.fullmatch, re.findall, re.finditer, re.sub, re.split; always raw strings for patterns (without r, '\b' becomes a backspace); character classes, quantifiers, greedy vs lazy (greedy .* eats too much), anchors, groups and named groups, alternation; flags IGNORECASE and VERBOSE; compiled patterns; 3.15's re.prefixmatch() replaces the soft-deprecated re.match(), whose start-only anchoring is a classic surprise; when not to use regex; an unbalanced ( gives re.PatternError: missing ), unterminated subpattern at position 0 (the class was named re.error before 3.13). (2) I19 text vs bytes as a message read aloud vs Morse code on a wire, the encoding being the codebook: str holds code points, bytes holds raw bytes; encode and decode; UTF-8 vs legacy encodings; UnicodeDecodeError and UnicodeEncodeError (decoding with the wrong codec gives UnicodeDecodeError: 'utf-8' codec can't decode byte ...); binary file modes rb and wb; bytearray; b'abc' + 'd' gives TypeError: can't concat str to bytes; Unicode normalization with unicodedata: len('é') is 1 in NFC and 2 in NFD and the two strings compare unequal; len of emoji and combining characters; casefold for comparisons (ch11); the UTF-8 default for open() in 3.15 (PEP 686; ch10's notebook) and opting out with PYTHONUTF8=0.

chapters.title: Preflight Checklist
chapters.scope: Recap pointers: ch14's pytest basics, edge cases, pytest.raises, approx, red-green-refactor and breakpoint(). (1) I20 testing in depth as a flight checklist run before every takeoff (commit): pytest fixtures; @pytest.mark.parametrize tables; tmp_path for files; capsys for testing printed output; monkeypatch and unittest.mock.patch (mocking the wrong import path does nothing); test isolation (a test that depends on another test's leftovers passes alone and fails in a suite); unittest.TestCase with setUp/tearDown and assertAlmostEqual; unit vs integration tests; coverage; test-driven development; doctest; property-based testing as awareness. (2) I21 code-quality tooling: PEP 8 and formatters (black, ruff format); linters (ruff, flake8); type checkers in the editor (ch21); docstring conventions; logging as a flight recorder you can turn up or down: levels, basicConfig, one logger per module, never print in libraries; logging.info('x') prints nothing because the default level is WARNING while logging.warning shows WARNING:root:shown; configuring logging after the first call does nothing; the warnings module; pdb in depth: commands and post-mortem with python -m pdb; breakpoint(); pre-commit hooks as awareness; reading tracebacks that carry ExceptionGroups and notes (ch22); print debugging left in production as a smell.

chapters.title: Waiters and Open Doors
chapters.scope: (1) I23 concurrency as a restaurant: threads are several waiters sharing one kitchen door (the GIL), processes are separate kitchens, asyncio is one waiter who never stands idle waiting for a dish; concurrency vs parallelism; I/O-bound vs CPU-bound; threading.Thread and join; the GIL and the free-threaded build (officially supported since 3.14, python3.15t); race conditions and Lock (a racy counter may print the right total by luck: our 4-thread run printed 400000 on both versions, so races are nondeterministic); queue.Queue; concurrent.futures ThreadPoolExecutor, ProcessPoolExecutor and as_completed; multiprocessing and why it needs the if __name__ == '__main__' guard (ch13); asyncio basics: async def, await, asyncio.run, gather, TaskGroup, asyncio.sleep; calling a coroutine without await prints <coroutine object g at 0x...> and RuntimeWarning: coroutine 'g' was never awaited; asyncio.run() inside a running loop gives RuntimeError: asyncio.run() cannot be called from a running event loop; subprocesses. (2) I25 programs that talk to the world, a shop with a front counter (stdin and arguments), a receipt printer (stdout), a complaints desk (stderr) and a back door to other shops (subprocess, HTTP): sys.argv; argparse (positional, optional, types, help); exit codes and sys.exit; stdin/stdout/stderr; environment variables; subprocess.run with a list of arguments (subprocess.run('ls -l') looks for a program literally named 'ls -l': FileNotFoundError: [Errno 2] No such file or directory: 'ls -l'); walking folders with pathlib.rglob and os.walk; CSV/JSON/XML in depth; sqlite3: connect, execute with ? placeholders, commit (building SQL with f-strings invites injection; forgetting conn.commit() loses writes, no error); urllib.request vs requests; calling a JSON web API; pickle dangers (never unpickle untrusted data); scheduling scripts. Close with a book-ending project: a small command-line tool that reads a folder or a CSV, stores results in SQLite and prints a report, with tests.
chapters.not_yet: Web frameworks, GUIs, data science libraries and async web servers (beyond this book; point to research section 5 'beyond intermediate').
chapters.visuals: (1) Restaurant picture with waiters, kitchens and one door, mapped to threads, processes and asyncio. (3) Race-condition tracer: two threads reading and writing one counter step by step, showing how an update is lost, then the Lock version (a teaching model; label it as such since the real run may not show the race). (4) Shop-counter picture for stdin/stdout/stderr/exit code with real terminals (data-exit) and an argparse machine turning a command line into a namespace; open-execute-commit-close reorder exercise for sqlite3.

chapters.capture_notes: Thread interleavings vary: either join and print in a fixed order or mark .nondet (never answer keys). No free-threaded python3.15t is installed here: describe it, do not run it. Use name.args for sys.argv/argparse runs and data-exit for exit codes; environment-variable demos need a name.cmd step. The capture environment passes no proxy variables, so internet HTTP calls will fail: serve JSON from a local http.server started inside the same program on 127.0.0.1 (or read a local file), and note that requests is installed only for 3.13.18. sqlite3: use a fixed database file recreated each run or ':memory:' so output is identical. Sort os.walk / rglob results before printing. ProcessPoolExecutor needs the __main__ guard and must finish within the 10 s run limit (30 s for a name.cmd last step).
